part.text:
Done. All 5 tests in `tests/robot-name.rs` pass (including the 4 `#[ignore]`d ones) and clippy is clean.

## What I did

**`src/lib.rs`** — the implementation:
- `Robot` owns its name as a `String`, so `name(&self) -> &str` is a plain safe borrow — no lifetime tricks needed.
- Uniqueness is enforced by one piece of global mutable state: `static USED_NAMES: LazyLock<Mutex<HashSet<String>>>` (std's `LazyLock`, no extra crate).
- `new()` and `reset_name()` draw names from `rand` (two letters from `A..=Z`, three digits from `0..=9`) in a retry loop until one isn't in the used set, then insert it. `reset_name()` first removes the old name so it isn't double-counted. The `Mutex` makes this safe under the parallel test threads.

**`Cargo.toml`** — added `rand = "0.9"` under `[dependencies]` (allowed by the spec; `rand` is on the OFFLINE_CRATES.md list). No test or other build files were touched.

## On the "better API design" question

Yes — the root problem is that `Robot::new()` takes no arguments, which hides the uniqueness invariant in process-wide statics. A cleaner design makes the registry an explicit value:

```rust
pub struct NameRegistry { used: HashSet<String>, /* + a PRNG */ }

impl Robot {
    pub fn new(registry: &mut NameRegistry) -> Self { ... }
}
```

The caller owns the registry (or holds a `&mut`/handle into it), so "every robot has a unique name" becomes a type-level guarantee instead of an undocumented global. You could even go further and have the registry hand out *tokens* (`struct NameToken(usize)` indexing into a `Vec<String>`), which would make `name(&self) -> &str` borrow-checkable without the robot storing a `String` at all. The trade-off is that the exercise's fixed signature (`Robot::new()` with zero args) is exactly what forces the global — which is the point of the exercise.

One deliberate quirk worth knowing: names of dropped robots are never returned to the pool, so the used-set only grows. That's safe (676,000 possible names vs. 3,529 robots in the test) and actually *more* conservative than the spec requires — the spec only demands uniqueness among *existing* robots.
